paragraphs: An agent making repeated decisions must balance choosing actions that currently look rewarding against exploring actions that could prove better. The standard multi-armed bandit setting ties new payoff observations to the actions the agent selects. This paper studies a broader setting where extra information about any action can arrive throughout the decision process, without a previously known arrival pattern.

The authors characterize how these information flows affect regret, the performance loss associated with learning which actions to choose. They establish matching lower and upper bounds, connecting the best achievable regret rate to the information available over time. This makes the arrival of information part of the problem's difficulty rather than merely an incidental benefit.

Their adaptive policy adjusts exploration using dynamically customized virtual time indexes. These indexes respond to information that has actually arrived. Without knowing the arrival process beforehand, the policy attains the regret rate achievable with that advance knowledge. The result concerns matching rates of performance, rather than claiming identical decisions or payoffs at every step.
neurips-2018-adaptive-learning-with-unkn.tldr: An adaptive bandit policy uses arriving side information to match the regret rate achievable when information flows are known beforehand.

paragraphs: Probabilistic inference often requires deriving conditional distributions or removing variables to obtain marginal distributions. Conjugacy relationships can make these calculations tractable, but identifying and applying them by hand can take time and introduce mistakes. Autoconj addresses this derivation work by recognizing useful mathematical structure in a model's computational description.

The system operates on Python functions that calculate a joint distribution's logarithm. This places the full log-joint computation at the center of the analysis, rather than restricting attention to relationships between pairs of random variables. Users can therefore express the relevant computation in Python without adopting a separate language specifically designed to describe conjugate models.

The proposed strategy supports inference algorithms that exploit conjugacy within Python-embedded probabilistic programming languages. Its significance is that model structure already present in executable code can help automate distributional derivations. The authors present this as a way to accelerate development of new inference algorithms and modeling strategies that take advantage of structure. They also provide a downloadable implementation of the system.
neurips-2018-autoconj-recognizing-and-ex.tldr: Autoconj automates conjugacy-based distribution derivations directly from Python functions that compute log-joint probabilities.

paragraphs: A model trained on labeled examples from one domain can perform poorly when its inputs come from another distribution. Unsupervised domain adaptation addresses this situation using labeled source examples and unlabeled target examples. One common approach makes the two domains' feature distributions resemble each other, but this overall match does not guarantee that examples belonging to corresponding classes are aligned.

The paper proposes constructing several diverse feature spaces and aligning source and target distributions separately within each one. It then encourages these different alignments to agree on the class predictions they assign to unlabeled target examples. Agreement therefore constrains the alignment process through its predictive consequences, alongside the matching of feature distributions.

The method is presented as a generic addition to approaches that already use domain alignment. The authors apply it to a recent state-of-the-art method and report significant improvements on several adaptation benchmarks. These results support the usefulness of combining diverse alignments with prediction agreement; the abstract does not claim that agreement guarantees correct class alignment in every setting.
neurips-2018-co-regularized-alignment-fo.tldr: Aligning domains in multiple feature spaces while encouraging prediction agreement improves the tested unsupervised adaptation method.

paragraphs: PAC-Bayes analysis gives bounds on how a learned predictor generalizes beyond its training data. A well-chosen prior can incorporate knowledge about the learning procedure and data distribution, potentially tightening those bounds. Choosing such a prior is difficult when the underlying distribution is unknown and the available information comes from the training data itself.

This paper shows that a prior selected from data through a differentially private mechanism yields a valid PAC-Bayes bound. It also develops a route for certain non-private prior-selection mechanisms to produce generalization bounds. The contribution is therefore a way to justify informative data-dependent priors while accounting for how their selection uses the data.

As an application, the authors choose a Gaussian prior's mean using stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics. Validity follows from controlling its 2-Wasserstein distance to a differentially private stationary distribution. Empirical evaluations show that the resulting bounds can be nonvacuous when other distribution-dependent bounds are vacuous, meaning they can provide informative guarantees in those tested circumstances.
neurips-2018-data-dependent-pac-bayes-pr.tldr: Differential privacy provides a route to valid PAC-Bayes bounds with data-dependent priors, including some priors selected non-privately.

paragraphs: Variational autoencoders can use binary hidden variables to represent data, with a Boltzmann machine supplying a powerful prior over those variables. Training such discrete models presents a particular obstacle: previous approaches with these priors used the evidence lower bound rather than the tighter importance-weighted bound. This paper develops relaxations that make the latter training objective available.

The authors introduce two ways to turn Boltzmann machines into continuous distributions for this purpose. One uses generalized overlapping transformations, and the other uses the Gaussian integral trick. Both approaches connect a discrete prior to a continuous formulation that permits importance-weighted training, expanding the training options for this family of latent-variable models.

Experiments on MNIST and OMNIGLOT show that models using these relaxations outperform previous discrete variational autoencoders with Boltzmann priors. The findings support the proposed relaxations as useful tools for this specific model family. The authors also make an implementation available that reproduces the reported results, connecting the mathematical proposals to an executable training approach.
neurips-2018-dvae-discrete-variational-a.tldr: Two continuous relaxations of Boltzmann priors enable importance-weighted training and improve the tested discrete variational autoencoders.

paragraphs: Entropy rate measures uncertainty in a sequence when successive observations may depend on one another. This paper studies estimating it from a single observed path of a stationary, reversible Markov chain with S states. The central question is how much data is needed when the state space is large and observations are dependent.

The authors prove that consistent estimation is achievable with n much larger than S²/log S when relaxation time is at most O(S/ln³ S). They also establish an impossibility result at sample sizes on the order of S²/log S or smaller when relaxation time is at least 1 + Ω(ln² S/√S). Under both conditions, optimal estimation accuracy scales as Θ(S²/(n log S)).

The empirical entropy-rate estimator requires at least order S² samples for consistency, even for memoryless chains. The proposed optimal estimators therefore improve sample requirements in the stated regime. Alongside synthetic experiments, the authors apply them to English-language corpora, linking entropy-rate estimation to perplexity and a benchmark for language modeling.
neurips-2018-entropy-rate-estimation-for.tldr: Under stated mixing and dependence conditions, Markov-chain entropy rates can be estimated optimally with sample requirements scaling as S²/log S.

paragraphs: Generalization requires reusing learned relationships when the particular entities involved change. Inspired by the hippocampal-entorhinal system, this paper proposes separating representations of entities from representations of how those entities relate. The aim is to preserve reusable structure while allowing the specific contents of an experience to vary across situations.

The authors build neural networks with hierarchy and fast Hebbian memory around this principle. They show that these networks can learn statistical patterns in memories and generalize structural knowledge. Spatial representations resembling those observed in the brain emerge in the models, suggesting that spatial cognition may reflect organizing principles with applications beyond physical space.

The work also interprets multiple entorhinal cell types as basis functions for constructing graphs of possible transitions, and shows that these representations use memories effectively. Experiments support a model assumption by finding a preserved relationship between entorhinal grid cells and hippocampal place cells across environments. This evidence connects the proposed computational separation to an observed relationship in the biological system.
neurips-2018-generalisation-of-structura.tldr: Separating relational structure from entity representations enables structural generalization in memory-based networks and yields brain-like spatial representations.

paragraphs: This paper studies global convergence for Langevin-based algorithms applied to nonconvex objectives made from n component functions. Its analytical strategy directly examines ergodicity of the numerical algorithms: their long-run distributional behavior. This provides a unified way to analyze gradient Langevin dynamics, its stochastic-gradient version, and a variance-reduced stochastic version.

The guarantees target an almost minimizer, defined here as a point within a ball around a global minimizer whose radius is O(d log(β + 1)/β). The dimension d and inverse temperature β therefore enter the stated target. The bounds also depend on the spectral gap λ of the Markov chain generated by gradient Langevin dynamics, making that chain's behavior consequential for the complexity guarantees.

The authors improve previously known gradient-evaluation bounds for both gradient and stochastic-gradient Langevin dynamics. They also give a first global convergence guarantee for the variance-reduced version, whose bound improves on the other two across a wide parameter regime. The result establishes parameter-dependent advantages rather than a claim that variance reduction is always faster.
neurips-2018-global-convergence-of-lange.tldr: Direct analysis of numerical Langevin dynamics yields improved global convergence bounds and a guarantee for its variance-reduced variant.

paragraphs: Boltzmann machines can represent complex, multimodal distributions over discrete variables, making them attractive priors for variational autoencoders. Discrete units, however, prevent direct use of the reparameterization trick needed for low-noise backpropagation. Although the Gumbel trick relaxes discrete variables into a trainable continuous formulation, its existing form is incompatible with Boltzmann-machine priors.

GumBolt extends the Gumbel approach to accommodate those priors. The purpose is to combine expressive dependencies among discrete latent variables with a relaxation suitable for gradient-based training. The authors describe their model as substantially simpler than recently proposed methods using Boltzmann priors, while also reporting a considerable performance improvement over those methods.

On permutation-invariant MNIST and OMNIGLOT, GumBolt achieves state-of-the-art performance within the specified class of models using only discrete latent variables. Its training also supports multiple-sample, importance-weighted estimation of log-likelihood, which the abstract says previous models could not use. Allowing that training approach further improves performance, giving the method both a modeling benefit and an additional training capability.
neurips-2018-gumbolt-extending-gumbel-tr.tldr: GumBolt adapts the Gumbel trick to Boltzmann priors, improving discrete-latent VAEs and enabling importance-weighted training.

paragraphs: An optimization algorithm can be good at reducing an objective without being equally efficient at making its gradient small. This paper emphasizes that distinction for stochastic gradient descent. Even for convex stochastic objectives, where standard SGD has an optimal objective-minimization rate, its rate for finding a point with a small gradient is not optimal.

For convex objectives, the authors introduce SGD3. It reaches gradient norm ε at a near-optimal rate of roughly ε to the power −2, with logarithmic factors suppressed. This improves the previous best rate of ε to the power −8/3. The contribution concerns the work needed to meet a gradient-based target, rather than simply lowering the objective.

For nonconvex objectives, SGD5 finds an ε-approximate local minimum at a rate of roughly ε to the power −3.5, improving the previous SGD-variant rate of roughly ε to the power −4. The authors also state that this rate is no slower than the best known stochastic Newton method across all parameter regimes. The nonconvex target remains an approximate local minimum.
neurips-2018-how-to-make-the-gradients-s.tldr: SGD3 and SGD5 improve theoretical rates for finding small gradients in convex problems and approximate local minima in nonconvex problems.

paragraphs: Neural networks make approximate posterior distributions flexible, but that flexibility complicates controlling which information a learned representation contains. In particular, structural requirements such as independence can be difficult to impose or assess. This paper adds information constraints to representation learning based on Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes.

The framework uses kernel-based independence measures to constrain the space of representations considered during learning. Its specific tool is the d-variable Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion, or dHSIC, which is used to enforce independence between latent representations and nuisance factors. This connects a desired statistical property of the representation directly to the learning process, rather than relying only on the neural network's expressive capacity.

The authors apply the framework to learning invariant and interpretable representations. They also present an application to single-cell RNA sequencing, where biological information is entangled with sequencing errors and sampling effects. Their method outperforms the state of the art in that domain. The application illustrates why controlling dependence on nuisance factors can matter when the useful signal and measurement-related effects are mixed together.
neurips-2018-information-constraints-on-.tldr: Kernel-based independence constraints help variational models learn representations separated from nuisance factors, with strong results in single-cell RNA sequencing.

paragraphs: The size of a gradient-based update determines how far a learning algorithm moves at each training step. L4 proposes adapting this size using the loss function itself. It rescales the gradient to aim for a fixed amount of predicted progress on the loss, tying the update magnitude directly to a prediction about the training objective.

The distinction between predicted and realized progress matters: the scheme sets a target based on its loss-based calculation. The authors apply the adaptation to Adam and Momentum, showing that it can enhance existing optimizers. This makes the proposal an adjustment to how updates are scaled within familiar training methods.

Across the reported experiments, the enhanced optimizers with default hyperparameters consistently outperform constant-stepsize counterparts, including the best ones tested, without a measurable increase in computational cost. Evaluation covers dense networks, convolutional networks, residual networks, and a recurrent Differential Neural Computer on datasets including MNIST, fashion MNIST, and CIFAR10. These findings support the practical usefulness of loss-based adaptation across the tested architectures and tasks.
neurips-2018-l4-practical-loss-based-ste.tldr: L4 rescales optimizer updates using predicted loss progress and improves Adam and Momentum across the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Determining whether two questions have similar meanings requires a representation of their intent and a way to compare those representations. This paper represents each question as a normal distribution in a continuous hidden space. It extends the idea behind Word Mover's Distance, replacing collections of embedded words with distributions that represent entire questions.

A variational autoencoder first learns to repeat and reformulate questions, using those tasks to infer distributions over their hidden intents. A variational siamese framework then learns semantic similarity discriminatively through the Wasserstein-2 distance. The comparison is framed as the minimum transport needed to move one question's intent distribution into agreement with the other's.

The resulting method achieves competitive performance on the Quora duplicate-questions dataset among models that process sentences individually. That qualification defines the comparison group for the reported result. More broadly, the work demonstrates a way to combine generative representation learning with a meaningful distance between distributions, so semantic similarity is expressed through the geometry of learned intent distributions.
neurips-2018-learning-semantic-similarit.tldr: The method represents question intents as normal distributions and learns semantic similarity through Wasserstein-2 transport distance.

paragraphs: Misinformation containment seeks to limit the spread of false information by launching competing campaigns in a social network. This paper examines the problem when an arbitrary number of information cascades can coexist. That setting makes interactions among campaigns central to deciding how a containment effort should operate.

The authors introduce a formal model of multi-cascade diffusion and a concept called cascade priority. They also describe several types of priority that they identify as common in real social networks. This gives the analysis a way to distinguish different forms of competition between spreading campaigns, rather than treating every cascade interaction as interchangeable.

The paper establishes a strong conditional hardness-of-approximation result for the general containment problem: the stated polynomial-time approximation is unavailable unless NP is contained in the specified quasipolynomial deterministic-time class. Alongside that theoretical obstacle, the authors develop algorithms and report encouraging experimental results. The two findings address different questions: the difficulty of broad computational guarantees and the observed effectiveness of the proposed algorithms.
neurips-2018-on-misinformation-containme.tldr: A multi-cascade model exposes strong conditional computational barriers to misinformation containment and supports algorithms with encouraging experimental results.

paragraphs: Online optimization makes decisions repeatedly while balancing objective performance against constraints. Earlier long-term constraint formulations add signed constraint values across time. Under that accounting, a decision comfortably inside the feasible region can offset a violation elsewhere, potentially hiding how much actual violation occurred during the sequence.

This paper instead sums squared positive violations. Feasible decisions contribute no negative credit, and squaring gives large violations greater weight. The proposed algorithms bound this cumulative quantity by O(T to the power 1 − β), with β between zero and one. Because this grows more slowly than the number of rounds T, the average squared positive violation decreases with the horizon.

The authors also derive bounds for constraint violation at an individual step. Their regret bounds generalize existing results for convex objectives and improve results for strongly convex objectives. Numerical experiments show the algorithm tracking the constraint boundary closely and accumulating little violation. Together, these results address objective performance while using a constraint measure that cannot erase violations through cancellation.
neurips-2018-online-convex-optimization-.tldr: The proposed online algorithms control squared positive constraint violations, preventing feasible decisions from canceling earlier violations.

paragraphs: Recommending one person to another requires satisfying both sides of a potential match. A recommendation can suit its recipient while failing because the suggested person has no reciprocal interest. This paper studies how to learn such mutual preferences sequentially, treating reciprocal recommendation as a distinct problem from recommending passive items.

The authors identify general limits on what a learning procedure can achieve, then formulate assumptions that make effective learning possible. Under those assumptions, they construct and analyze a computationally efficient algorithm for discovering mutual likes. The theoretical benchmark is a clairvoyant algorithm that already knows every user's preferences, providing a demanding reference for the discovery rate.

The proposed algorithm uncovers mutual likes at a pace comparable to that benchmark within the stated framework and assumptions. This is a conditional performance guarantee, not a claim about every possible preference pattern. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets also show improvements over simple baselines, giving empirical support alongside the theoretical analysis of learning mutual interest.
neurips-2018-online-reciprocal-recommend.tldr: Under stated learning assumptions, an efficient reciprocal recommender discovers mutual likes at a pace comparable to an all-knowing benchmark.

paragraphs: Financial returns can have heavy tails whose behavior changes over time and differs between the positive and negative sides. This paper proposes a compact quantile-regression framework for learning those dynamics. The target is the conditional distribution of returns, particularly its tail quantiles, rather than a description based only on volatility.

The model combines an LSTM sequence model with a newly constructed parametric quantile function. The sequence component captures temporal behavior, while the quantile function represents the conditional return distribution. The authors state that the model captures serial dependence in higher moments individually, allowing its account of changing distributional shape to extend beyond changing variance.

Across a wide range of asset classes, out-of-sample forecasts of conditional quantiles or value at risk outperform the GARCH family. The approach also avoids quantile crossing, where estimated quantiles would be ordered inconsistently, and the ill-posedness identified in comparison with a parametric probability-density approach. These findings concern the reported forecasting task and the structure of its distributional representation.
neurips-2018-parsimonious-quantile-regre.tldr: An LSTM paired with a parametric quantile function captures changing return tails and improves reported quantile forecasts over GARCH models.

paragraphs: Mobile vision systems must work within limited computing and memory resources. This paper argues that efficient architecture design should account for how well operations are implemented in deep-learning frameworks. It proposes PeleeNet, a network built from conventional convolutions, motivated by implementation inefficiencies affecting the depthwise separable convolutions used by several lightweight architectures.

On ImageNet ILSVRC 2012, the authors report higher accuracy and 1.8-times faster execution than MobileNet and MobileNetV2 on NVIDIA TX2. PeleeNet is also 66% of MobileNet's model size. They then combine PeleeNet with Single Shot MultiBox Detector and further optimize the architecture to create the Pelee object-detection system.

Pelee achieves 76.4% mean average precision on PASCAL VOC2007 and 22.4 on MS COCO, with reported speeds of 23.6 frames per second on iPhone 8 and 125 on NVIDIA TX2. On COCO, it exceeds YOLOv2's precision while using 13.6-times lower computational cost and an 11.3-times smaller model. These results connect architecture choices to measured efficiency on the specified devices.
neurips-2018-pelee-a-real-time-object-de.tldr: Pelee combines a conventional-convolution backbone with an optimized SSD detector to deliver accurate, real-time detection on the tested mobile hardware.

paragraphs: Vehicle routing requires constructing routes that satisfy operational constraints while achieving a good objective value. This paper trains a single reinforcement-learning policy to produce near-optimal routes across a broad range of similarly sized instances. Training uses reward signals and feasibility rules, allowing the model to learn a route-construction strategy.

The approach represents that strategy as a parameterized stochastic policy and optimizes it with policy gradients. Once trained, the model generates a solution as a sequence of consecutive actions in real time. It does not require retraining for each new instance, so the learned policy can be reused within the class of problems it addresses.

For medium-sized capacitated routing instances, the method produces better solutions than classical heuristics and Google's OR-Tools with comparable computation time after training. The authors also demonstrate split deliveries and examine their effect on solution quality. They identify stochastic routing as another applicable variant and describe broader combinatorial optimization as a potential direction, rather than reporting that broader capability as an established result.
neurips-2018-reinforcement-learning-for-.tldr: A reusable reinforcement-learning policy constructs strong vehicle routes in real time for similarly sized instances after training.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a policy would perform using experience gathered under another policy. This paper considers accuracy for both individual policy values and average policy values. That dual focus asks the evaluation procedure to capture individual outcomes as well as aggregate performance, rather than assessing only the overall average.

Drawing inspiration from causal reasoning, the authors derive a finite-sample generalization-error bound for value estimates produced by Markov decision process models. They then use this upper bound as a learning objective. The resulting algorithm learns an MDP model with a balanced representation, connecting its representation-learning criterion directly to an analysis of policy-value estimation error.

The authors show that the approach can substantially reduce mean squared error on common synthetic benchmarks and in an HIV treatment simulation domain. These findings support using the error bound to guide model learning for off-policy evaluation. The simulation result is evidence about policy-value estimation in that domain; the stated outcome is lower estimation error, rather than a demonstrated improvement in real-world treatment.
neurips-2018-representation-balancing-md.tldr: A causal-inspired error bound guides balanced MDP representation learning and can substantially improve off-policy value estimation.

paragraphs: Semantic scene completion predicts both which parts of a three-dimensional volume are occupied and which object categories occupy them. These predictions provide information that an intelligent agent can use to understand its surroundings. This paper organizes the task into a sequence of distinct stages, making intermediate semantic interpretation an explicit part of the process.

The framework first performs two-dimensional semantic segmentation, then reprojects that information into three dimensions, and finally completes the three-dimensional semantic scene. The authors identify explicit segmentation as a significant source of improved performance. The separation also allows flexible combinations of sensor data and creates opportunities for improvements in individual subtasks to benefit the overall system.

Experiments show high-quality completion from either a single depth input or RGB-D input. The framework outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on both synthetic and real datasets. These findings support the proposed decomposition as an effective architecture for the tested scene-completion settings, while the modular stages explain how it can accommodate sensor fusion and advances in its component tasks.
neurips-2018-see-and-think-disentangling.tldr: Separating segmentation, reprojection, and 3D completion improves semantic scene reconstruction from depth or RGB-D inputs.

paragraphs: Regression models predict numerical outputs, but obtaining enough labeled examples to train a deep model can be expensive or impossible. This paper proposes semi-supervised deep kernel learning, or SSDKL, to make use of examples whose output values are unavailable. Its central mechanism is to minimize predictive variance within a posterior-regularization framework.

The model combines neural networks' ability to learn hierarchical representations with Gaussian processes' probabilistic modeling capabilities. This pairing supplies both learned features and a predictive distribution. Unlabeled data enter through the variance-based learning criterion, giving those examples a role in shaping the model even though they do not supply target values for ordinary supervised regression.

The authors evaluate SSDKL on a diverse collection of real-world regression tasks. They report improvements over supervised deep kernel learning and over VAT and mean teacher methods adapted for regression. The findings support predictive-variance minimization as a useful way to incorporate unlabeled data in these tasks, connecting probabilistic prediction to the practical problem of limited labeled training data.
neurips-2018-semi-supervised-deep-kernel.tldr: SSDKL combines neural representations and Gaussian processes, using predictive variance to learn from unlabeled regression examples.

paragraphs: Softmax converts a neural network's outputs into a categorical probability distribution. In language modeling, this final transformation can limit the distributions the network can represent, creating a softmax bottleneck. This paper investigates that restriction by analyzing the set of outputs that log-softmax can produce.

The analysis identifies the cause of the bottleneck and motivates an alternative output activation called sigsoftmax. Its construction combines an exponential function with a sigmoid through multiplication. The proposed activation can break the representational bottleneck without introducing additional parameters, making the form of the output transformation itself the central change.

Language-modeling experiments compare sigsoftmax with softmax and a mixture of sigsoftmax with a mixture of softmax. The proposed versions outperform their corresponding alternatives in those experiments. The work therefore offers both an explanation of a representational restriction and empirical evidence that changing the output activation can help. Its parameter-free modification targets a limitation at the probability-output stage rather than requiring a larger parameter count.
neurips-2018-sigsoftmax-reanalysis-of-th.tldr: Sigsoftmax can break the softmax representational bottleneck without extra parameters and improves the reported language-modeling results.

paragraphs: A generative network transforms input noise into an output distribution. This paper examines what such transformations require from the network, focusing on the relationship between network size, noise dimensionality, and the distributions being produced. Its contributions are explicit constructions and analyses of their efficiency.

First, the authors construct ReLU networks that increase noise dimensionality using a space-filling function built from iterated tent maps. They establish optimality of this construction by studying how many affine pieces multivariate ReLU networks can produce. This connects the complexity of the distributional transformation to the piecewise-affine structure of the functions computed by the network.

Second, they give efficient transformations between one-dimensional uniform and normal distributions using a number of nodes polynomial in log(1/ε). These constructions use Taylor approximation and a binary-search component for computing inverse functions. Finally, the paper indicates how high-dimensional distributions can be transformed efficiently into lower-dimensional ones. Together, the results clarify several ways network structure can compensate for differences in the form and dimensionality of input noise.
neurips-2018-size-noise-tradeoffs-in-gen.tldr: Explicit network constructions characterize efficient transformations of noise distributions, including an optimal ReLU construction for increasing dimensionality.

paragraphs: Predicting visual-cortex activity during natural video could help researchers study how the brain processes realistic input. The authors develop a deep recurrent network that predicts inferred spiking activity from thousands of mouse V1 neurons recorded simultaneously using two-photon microscopy. It also accounts for gaze position and brain-state changes associated with running and pupil dilation.

A model used for simulated experiments needs to work beyond the stimulus statistics encountered during training. The paper therefore tests transfer between natural stimuli and artificial noise. A model trained on natural images correctly predicts neurons' orientation tuning in response to artificial noise stimuli, showing transfer of this particular response property.

For broader transfer from natural movies to noise, the authors fine-tune only the final layer's weights while keeping the rest of the movie-trained network fixed. This maintains high predictive performance in both domains. The reverse transfer does not work in the same way. That asymmetry is a stated finding and matters when choosing training stimuli for models intended to support experiments across stimulus types.
neurips-2018-stimulus-domain-transfer-in.tldr: A recurrent cortical-response model transfers from natural movies to noise through final-layer fine-tuning, but the reverse transfer does not hold.
